a: They hoped that as Peter went by, his shadow at least would pass over some of them.
p: Codex Bezae and some allies add that the sick were in fact set free from their illnesses.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.orig: ἵνα ἐρχομένου Πέτρου κἂν ἡ σκιὰ ἐπισκιάσῃ τινὶ αὐτῶν.
readings.en: so that as Peter came, even his shadow might overshadow some of them.
readings.plain: They hoped that as Peter went by, his shadow at least would pass over some of them.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, about 400) with some Old Latin and Vulgate manuscripts (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: ... ἀπηλλάσσοντο γὰρ ἀπὸ πάσης ἀσθενείας ὡς εἶχεν ἕκαστος αὐτῶν.
readings.en: ... for they were set free from every sickness, whatever each of them had.
readings.plain: They hoped that as Peter went by, his shadow at least would pass over some of them. For they were set free from every sickness that each of them had.

why: The addition is found only in the Western witnesses. It looks like an explanation added to make clear that the hope was not in vain. Luke himself leaves the shadow's effect unstated and says in the next verse that all were healed.
b: This is one of many places in Acts where Codex Bezae, the main witness to the "Western" text, adds a clause. The Western text of Acts is about eight to nine percent longer than the text in most English Bibles.

a: put them in the public lockup.
p: Codex Bezae adds that after the arrest each of the leaders went home.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts; also the Byzantine text
readings.orig: καὶ ἔθεντο αὐτοὺς ἐν τηρήσει δημοσίᾳ.
readings.en: and put them in public custody.
readings.plain: put them in the public lockup.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, about 400) and some Old Latin witnesses (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: ... καὶ ἐπορεύθη εἷς ἕκαστος εἰς τὰ ἴδια.
readings.en: ... and each one went to his own home.
readings.plain: put them in the public lockup. Then each of them went home.

why: Only Western witnesses have the clause. It adds a vivid touch (compare the similar line in John 7:53) but has no support in the older Alexandrian manuscripts.

a: the commander of the temple and the chief priests
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add the high priest (Greek "the priest") to those who were baffled.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.orig: ὅ τε στρατηγὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ καὶ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς
readings.en: both the commander of the temple and the chief priests
readings.plain: the commander of the temple and the chief priests

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "the high priest and the captain of the temple and the chief priests"
readings.orig: ὅ τε ἱερεὺς καὶ ὁ στρατηγὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ καὶ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς
readings.en: both the priest and the commander of the temple and the chief priests
readings.plain: the high priest, the commander of the temple and the chief priests

why: The shorter list is in the critical editions. The high priest has just been named (5:21), and a scribe likely added him here; "the priest" alone for the high priest is an Old Testament usage.

a: We ordered you, and ordered you firmly, to stop teaching in this name.
p: Many manuscripts add "not," turning the high priest's words into a question: "Didn't we order you...?"

readings.w: SBLGNT; Papyrus 74 (600s), Sinaiticus (first hand), Alexandrinus, Vaticanus (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: Παραγγελίᾳ παρηγγείλαμεν ὑμῖν μὴ διδάσκειν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι τούτῳ
readings.en: With an order we ordered you not to teach in this name
readings.plain: We ordered you, and ordered you firmly, to stop teaching in this name.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (corrector), Bezae, the Byzantine majority and Textus Receptus (KJV "Did not we straitly command you"); NA28 prints the word in brackets
readings.en: Did we not order you with an order ...?
readings.plain: Didn't we order you, and order you firmly, to stop teaching in this name?

why: The oldest manuscripts have no "not." A scribe could easily have added it to make the sentence a question, as in 4:17–18; the meaning is the same either way.
b: "With an order we ordered you" is a Semitic way of putting a verb twice for force, common in the Greek Old Testament. This translation gives it as "We ordered you, and ordered you firmly."

a: We ourselves are witnesses of these events.
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "his": "we are his witnesses."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.orig: καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν μάρτυρες τῶν ῥημάτων τούτων
readings.en: and we are witnesses of these things
readings.plain: We ourselves are witnesses of these events.

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV, "we are his witnesses of these things")
readings.orig: καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν αὐτοῦ μάρτυρες τῶν ῥημάτων τούτων
readings.en: and we are his witnesses of these things
readings.plain: We ourselves are his witnesses of these events.

why: The critical editions print the shorter text. "His" makes plain whose witnesses the apostles are; the sense is the same, since the apostles are Jesus' witnesses throughout Acts (1:8).

a: they wanted to kill the apostles
p: Some editions and the KJV read "they took counsel" instead of "they wanted."

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House, NA27, the Byzantine text
readings.en: they wanted to kill them
readings.plain: they wanted to kill the apostles

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "took counsel to slay them"); NA28 as recorded in the STEPBible word list
readings.en: they were planning to kill them
readings.plain: they made plans to kill the apostles

why: The two verbs differ by two letters. The base text and most editions read "wanted"; either reading leaves the council ready to kill until Gamaliel speaks.

a: take the men out
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read "the apostles."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.en: the men
readings.plain: take the men out

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "to put the apostles forth a little space"
readings.en: the apostles
readings.plain: take the apostles out

why: Gamaliel's distant word "the men" fits his speech, which calls them "these men" (5:35, 38). A scribe replaced it with the more respectful title.

a: you will not be able to tear them down.
p: Codex Bezae expands Gamaliel's warning. The Byzantine text reads "it" for "them."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.en: you will not be able to overthrow them
readings.plain: you will not be able to tear them down.

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "ye cannot overthrow it"
readings.en: you cannot overthrow it
readings.plain: you cannot tear it down.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, about 400) and some allies (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: οὐ δυνήσεσθε καταλῦσαι αὐτούς, οὔτε ὑμεῖς οὔτε βασιλεῖς οὔτε τύραννοι· ἀπέχεσθε οὖν ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τούτων
readings.en: you will not be able to overthrow them, neither you nor kings nor tyrants; so keep away from these men
readings.plain: you will not be able to tear them down, not you, not kings, not tyrants. So keep away from these men.

why: The critical text is shortest and has the best early support. The Byzantine "it" matches "this plan or this work" in 5:38; the critical "them" means the apostles. The Western addition repeats 5:38 and heightens the warning, a typical Western expansion.

a: for the sake of the Name
p: The oldest manuscripts say only "the Name." Later copies add "of Jesus" or "his."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.en: for the name
readings.plain: for the sake of the Name

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "for his name")
readings.en: for his name
readings.plain: for the sake of his name

readings.w: Byzantine majority text
readings.en: for the name of Jesus
readings.plain: for the sake of the name of Jesus

why: The bare "the Name" is unusual, and scribes filled it out in different ways, which is a sign that the short form is original. Early Christians spoke of "the Name" as Jews spoke of God's name (compare 3 John 7).

a: the Messiah is Jesus
t: "The Messiah is Jesus" or "Jesus is the Messiah"
p: The word order differs. The KJV reads "to preach Jesus Christ."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.en: the Christ, Jesus
readings.plain: the Messiah is Jesus

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "to preach Jesus Christ"
readings.en: Jesus the Christ
readings.plain: Jesus is the Messiah

why: The critical order puts "the Messiah" first: the apostles' message to Jews was that the Messiah they awaited is Jesus. The later order reads more like a name.

a: full of the Spirit and wisdom
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read "the Holy Spirit."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.en: full of the Spirit and wisdom
readings.plain: full of the Spirit and wisdom

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom"
readings.en: full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom
readings.plain: full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom

why: Scribes often added "Holy" to "Spirit," as in 6:5. The meaning does not change.

a: full of grace and power
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read "full of faith and power."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.en: full of grace and power
readings.plain: full of grace and power

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "full of faith and power"
readings.en: full of faith and power
readings.plain: full of faith and power

why: "Faith" probably came in from 6:5, where Stephen is "full of faith and the Holy Spirit." The older manuscripts read "grace," which links Stephen with the apostles' "great grace" (4:33).

a: They were no match for the wisdom and the Spirit he spoke with.
p: Codex Bezae adds that Stephen refuted them boldly, and that they could not face the truth.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts; also the Byzantine text
readings.orig: καὶ οὐκ ἴσχυον ἀντιστῆναι τῇ σοφίᾳ καὶ τῷ πνεύματι ᾧ ἐλάλει.
readings.en: and they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit with which he spoke.
readings.plain: They were no match for the wisdom and the Spirit he spoke with.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, about 400) and some Old Latin and Syriac witnesses (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: ... διὰ τὸ ἐλέγχεσθαι αὐτοὺς ἐπ' αὐτοῦ μετὰ πάσης παρρησίας. μὴ δυνάμενοι οὖν ἀντοφθαλμεῖν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ
readings.en: ... because they were refuted by him with all boldness. Being unable, then, to look the truth in the face,
readings.plain: They were no match for the wisdom and the Spirit he spoke with, because he refuted them boldly. They could not face the truth.

why: The addition is typical of the Western text, which fills in motives and links. It has no support in the older Alexandrian manuscripts.
b: Metzger also reports that Bezae changes the first half of the verse: "the wisdom that was in him, and the Holy Spirit with which he spoke." In Bezae the sentence about facing the truth runs on into 6:11.

a: keeps on talking against the holy place and the law
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "blasphemous words" and "this."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts (NA28 adds "this" in brackets)
readings.orig: οὐ παύεται λαλῶν ῥήματα κατὰ τοῦ τόπου τοῦ ἁγίου
readings.en: does not stop speaking words against the holy place and the law
readings.plain: keeps on talking against the holy place and the law

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place"
readings.orig: οὐ παύεται ῥήματα βλάσφημα λαλῶν κατὰ τοῦ τόπου τοῦ ἁγίου τούτου
readings.en: does not stop speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law
readings.plain: keeps on speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law

why: "Blasphemous" was likely brought in from 6:11. The shorter text has the older support.

a: Hamor's sons at Shechem
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV call Hamor "the father of Shechem," as in Genesis 33:19.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.en: the sons of Hamor in Shechem
readings.plain: Hamor's sons at Shechem

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "the sons of Emmor the father of Sychem"
readings.en: the sons of Hamor, of Shechem (his father or son)
readings.plain: the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem

why: The Byzantine "of Shechem" makes Shechem a person, as in Genesis 33:19 ("Hamor, Shechem's father"), and is probably a scribe's correction toward Genesis. The older reading names the place. Neither removes the difference from Genesis discussed in the note on this verse.

a: openly made
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say God "had sworn" the promise to Abraham.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.orig: ἧς ὡμολόγησεν ὁ θεὸς τῷ Ἀβραάμ
readings.en: which God declared to Abraham
readings.plain: openly made

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "which God had sworn to Abraham"
readings.orig: ἧς ὤμοσεν ὁ θεὸς τῷ Ἀβραάμ
readings.en: which God swore to Abraham
readings.plain: sworn

why: The verb homologeō ("declare, agree, promise openly") is the less expected word. "Swore" matches Genesis 22:16 and Luke 1:73 and is what a scribe would expect; the harder reading is more likely original.

a: until a different king rose to rule Egypt
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV lack "over Egypt": "another king arose."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 (in brackets), Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.en: another king arose over Egypt
readings.plain: until a different king rose to rule Egypt

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV, "another king arose, which knew not Joseph")
readings.en: another king arose
readings.plain: until a different king rose to power

why: Most editions print the words. NA28 brackets them because a scribe could have added them from the Greek of Exodus 1:8, which has "over Egypt"; or a scribe could have dropped them as unneeded after "in Egypt" in 7:17.

a: an angel appeared to him
t: "An angel" or "an angel of the Lord"
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "of the Lord," as in Exodus 3:2.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.en: an angel appeared to him
readings.plain: an angel appeared to him

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "an angel of the Lord"
readings.en: an angel of the Lord appeared to him
readings.plain: an angel of the Lord appeared to him

why: The addition matches Exodus 3:2. Scribes tended to bring quotations into line with the Old Testament.

a: Abraham and Isaac and Jacob
t: "The God of Isaac, the God of Jacob"
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV repeat "the God of" before each name, as Exodus 3:6 does.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.orig: ὁ θεὸς Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακώβ
readings.en: the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob
readings.plain: Abraham and Isaac and Jacob

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ὁ θεὸς Ἀβραὰμ καὶ ὁ θεὸς Ἰσαὰκ καὶ ὁ θεὸς Ἰακώβ
readings.en: the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob
readings.plain: Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob

why: The fuller form matches Exodus 3:6 and Matthew 22:32. The shorter form is the older and is the same as Peter's in 3:13.

a: 'God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, a prophet like me.'
p: The KJV adds "the Lord your God" and "him shall ye hear," from Deuteronomy 18:15.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.orig: Προφήτην ὑμῖν ἀναστήσει ὁ θεὸς ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὑμῶν ὡς ἐμέ.
readings.en: God will raise up a prophet for you from your brothers like me.
readings.plain: 'God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, a prophet like me.'

readings.w: Byzantine majority text
readings.orig: Προφήτην ὑμῖν ἀναστήσει κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὑμῶν ὡς ἐμέ.
readings.en: The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from your brothers like me.
readings.plain: 'The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, a prophet like me.'

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear")
readings.orig: Προφήτην ὑμῖν ἀναστήσει κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὑμῶν ὡς ἐμέ· αὐτοῦ ἀκούσεσθε.
readings.en: The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from your brothers like me; him you will hear.
readings.plain: 'The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, a prophet like me. You must listen to him.'

why: The shorter text is the older. The additions bring the quotation closer to Deuteronomy 18:15 and to Peter's fuller quotation in 3:22.

a: the star of the god Rephan
t: Rephan or Remphan, "the god" or "your god"
p: The name is spelled several ways in the manuscripts. The KJV has "your god Remphan."

readings.w: SBLGNT (NA28 and Tyndale House add "your" in brackets or text)
readings.en: the star of the god Raiphan
readings.plain: the star of the god Rephan

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "the star of your god Remphan"
readings.orig: τὸ ἄστρον τοῦ θεοῦ ὑμῶν Ῥεμφάν
readings.en: the star of your god Remphan
readings.plain: the star of your god Remphan

why: The spelling of this foreign name varied widely in copying. "Your" is in the Greek of Amos 5:26 and may have been added to match it; the editors disagree, and the meaning hardly changes.

a: the God of Jacob
t: "The God of Jacob" or "the house of Jacob"
p: A famous puzzle: did David ask to find a dwelling for God, or for the house of Jacob?

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, the Byzantine majority and Textus Receptus (KJV); Sinaiticus (corrector), Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, the Latin and Syriac versions (reported by Metzger)
readings.en: a dwelling for the God of Jacob
readings.plain: the God of Jacob

readings.w: NA27 and NA28; Papyrus 74, Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Bezae (reported by Metzger)
readings.en: a dwelling for the house of Jacob
readings.plain: the house of Jacob

why: This translation follows the SBLGNT and Tyndale House, which read "God." It fits Psalm 132:5, the verse Stephen echoes, and it gives "him" in 7:47 ("built him a house") a clear antecedent. The NA28 editors chose "house" as the harder reading, supported by very old manuscripts; they thought scribes changed it to match the psalm. Some scholars suspect an early copying slip in the Greek. If "house of Jacob" is right, David asked for a place for Israel's worship, a dwelling among the people.
b: The site's Psalm 132:5 reads "a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob."

a: does not make his home in what hands have made
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "temples": "dwelleth not in temples made with hands."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and Tyndale House, printing the reading of the older manuscripts
readings.orig: οὐχ ὁ ὕψιστος ἐν χειροποιήτοις κατοικεῖ
readings.en: the Most High does not dwell in things made with hands
readings.plain: does not make his home in what hands have made

readings.w: Byzantine majority text and Textus Receptus (KJV), "dwelleth not in temples made with hands"
readings.orig: οὐχ ὁ ὕψιστος ἐν χειροποιήτοις ναοῖς κατοικεῖ
readings.en: the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands
readings.plain: does not make his home in temples that hands have made

why: "Temples" was probably supplied from Paul's similar words in 17:24. The shorter text is older and, by leaving the noun out, puts the temple in the same class as any handmade object.
